pages.text: Bulgaria joins Eurozone

Bulgaria joins Eurozone



• Recently, Bulgaria adopted the euro on January 1, 2026,
becoming the 21st member of the eurozone.

• This marked a major step in Bulgaria’s economic
integration with the European Union.

• The adoption came nearly 20 years after Bulgaria joined
the EU in 2007.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

What is Euro?

• The euro (€) is the official currency used by 20 of the 27
European Union member countries, collectively known as the
eurozone.

• It was launched in 1999 for electronic payments and
banking, with physical coins and banknotes introduced in
2002.

• The euro replaced national currencies like the German
mark, French franc, Italian lira, and others in adopting
countries.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

• Several non-EU countries and territories, such as Kosovo and
Montenegro, also use the euro unofficially.

• The European Central Bank (ECB), headquartered in
Frankfurt, manages the euro’s monetary policy, controls
inflation, and sets interest rates.

• The ECB operates independently from national governments,
ensuring stable pricing and financial credibility across the
eurozone.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone



• Like the US Federal Reserve, the ECB influences
economic growth and stability through tools like open
market operations and interest rate decisions.

• The euro is the second most traded and held currency in
the world, after the US dollar.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

What is eurozone?

• The eurozone, officially called the euro area, is a geographic and
economic region made up of European Union (EU) countries that
have fully adopted the euro as their national currency.

• As of January 2026, the eurozone consists of 21 EU countries:
Austria, Belgium, Croatia, Cyprus, Estonia, Finland, France,
Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania,
Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Portugal, Slovakia,
Slovenia, Spain, and Bulgaria.

• Not all EU countries use the euro; some retain their own national
currencies to maintain monetary independence.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

• The European Central Bank (ECB) has exclusive authority to
formulate and implement monetary policy for all eurozone countries.
The ECB is headed by Christine Lagarde, who has served as
President since November 2019, succeeding Mario Draghi.

• The foundation of the eurozone was laid by the Maastricht Treaty
(1992), which created the EU and envisaged a common economic
and monetary union with a shared currency and central banking
system.

• Signatories included the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy,
France, Ireland, Belgium, Denmark, Spain, Portugal, Greece,
Netherlands, and Luxembourg.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

• The Maastricht Treaty also laid the foundation for the Economic and
Monetary Union (EMU) and proposed the introduction of a single currency,
the Euro. The treaty set strict criteria for EMU membership:
➢ budget deficits under 3% of GDP,
➢ public debt under 60% of GDP,
➢ exchange rate stability,
➢ inflation within 1.5% of the EU's three lowest inflation rates,
➢ long-term interest rates under 2%.

• Despite Italy and Belgium having debt ratios around 120%, they were
approved for EMU entry due to efforts to reduce their debt.

• In 1998, 11 countries officially joined the EMU, but the United Kingdom and
Sweden opted to delay their participation.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

• In September 2000, Denmark narrowly rejected
adopting the euro via a referendum.

• Greece initially failed to meet the economic requirements
but qualified after reforms and joined the EMU in January
2001.

• Only 12 countries were part of the single currency area --
including France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and Greece --
when the first euro bills and coins were rolled out on
January 1, 2002.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone


• It gradually widened with Slovenia joining in 2007, Cyprus
and Malta in 2008, Slovakia in 2009, Estonia in 2011,
Latvia in 2014 then Lithuania in 2015.

• Croatia was the last country to join in 2023, bringing the total
to 20.

• Although today all EU countries are part of the EMU, only 20
have replaced their national currencies with the euro, forming the
eurozone.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone


• Current eurozone countries are: Germany, Austria, France,
Belgium, Cyprus, Estonia, Finland, Italy, Portugal, Greece,
Ireland, Latvia, Spain, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta,
Slovakia, Slovenia, the Netherlands and Croatia.

• Non-euro area members that have not yet adopted the euro will do so
when conditions are met; most joined the EU in 2004, 2007, or
2013. These include: Bulgaria, Czechia, Hungary, Poland,
Romania, and Sweden.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone
How to join eurozone?

• To adopt the euro, an EU member state must meet certain
convergence criteria, which are economic and legal conditions set
out in the 1992 Maastricht Treaty.

• These are designed to ensure that the country is ready to integrate
into the eurozone without causing financial instability.

• The main economic criteria include:
➢ Price stability: The country’s average inflation rate over one year
   must not exceed that of the three best-performing EU countries
   by more than 1.5 percentage points.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

➢ Public finances: The government’s annual budget deficit must be below
  3% of GDP, and public debt must not exceed 60% of GDP.

➢ Interest rate durability: The country’s average long-term interest rate
  must not be more than 2 percentage points higher than those of the
  three best-performing EU member states.

➢ Exchange rate stability: The country must participate in the Exchange
  Rate Mechanism (ERM II) for at least 2 years, maintaining exchange
  rate stability without significant deviation or devaluation of its currency.

• Since 2018, countries entering ERM II must also engage in close
cooperation with the European Central Bank (ECB), including joining its
Single Supervisory Mechanism, and implementing specific policy reforms
as agreed upon.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

• Alongside these economic conditions, the country must also
ensure legal convergence. This means its national laws must be
compatible with the rules of the European System of Central
Banks (ESCB) and the ECB, especially regarding the
independence of the national central bank.

• The country’s readiness is assessed in a convergence report
published by both the European Central Bank and the
European Commission.

• These reports are issued at least once every two years for all
non-euro area EU members or sooner if a country specifically
requests euro adoption.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

• Based on these reports, the Council of the EU begins the
formal decision-making process. The Council needs:
➢ A proposal from the European Commission,
➢ A recommendation from euro area member states,
➢ An opinion from the European Parliament,
➢ And a discussion at the level of the European Council
   (heads of state/government).

• The final decision to allow a country to adopt the euro is made
by all EU member states. In EU law, this is called the
“abrogation of the derogation”.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

• Once the decision is approved, the Council of the EU, based on a
Commission proposal and after consulting the ECB, irrevocably
fixes the exchange rate at which the country’s national currency
will be replaced by the euro.

• This decision is made unanimously by the euro area countries
and the adopting country in the Council.

• Within six months of the Commission’s proposal, the euro area
countries must submit their recommendation on whether the
adopting country is ready. This recommendation must be supported
by a qualified majority of eurozone members.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone


• Once everything is finalized, the country begins the
transition to the euro. This includes public information
campaigns, banking and payment system adjustments, and
the gradual withdrawal of the national currency from
circulation.

• All EU countries (except Denmark, which has an opt-
out clause) are legally bound to adopt the euro once they
meet the required conditions. Denmark is not obligated but
may choose to apply in the future.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

What is happening recently?

• Bulgaria adopted the euro on January 1, 2026, officially
becoming the 21st member of the eurozone, nearly two decades
after joining the European Union in 2007.

• The Bulgarian lev and the euro will circulate together until
January 31, 2026; from February 1, 2026, the euro will be the
sole legal tender.

• During January 2026, payments made in lev must be returned
with change only in euros to speed up the transition.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

• President Rumen Radev described euro adoption as the
final step of EU integration.

• Public opinion remains divided, with around 49% opposing
the switch amid inflation concerns.

• Food prices rose about 5% year-on-year in late 2025, more
than twice the eurozone average, intensifying public fears.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

Efforts by Bulgaria –

• Bulgaria began working toward euro adoption soon after joining the
EU in 2007, as required by its accession treaty.

• These efforts were paused around 2010 due to the sovereign debt
crisis in Europe, which nearly bankrupted Greece and other eurozone
countries.

• From 2016 onward, Bulgaria renewed its push for eurozone
membership, arguing that adoption of the euro would help prevent the
country from being sidelined in EU decision-making and would
better integrate its export-oriented economy into the bloc.

Bulgaria joins Eurozone

• Since facing hyperinflation in the 1990s, Bulgaria has operated
under a currency board arrangement, where its currency, the lev,
is tightly pegged to the euro.

• As a result, Bulgaria’s monetary policy is already closely tied to the
European Central Bank (ECB), even though it has not officially
adopted the euro.

• In the previous year, Bulgaria's euro accession was delayed because
it failed to meet inflation targets, with price pressures rising due to
Europe’s energy crisis after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Somaliland’s Recognition

Somaliland’s Recognition


• Recently, Israel became the first country to formally recognise
Somaliland as an independent state, despite it not being UN-
recognised and claimed by Somalia.

• The decision may heighten regional tensions in the Horn of
Africa and strain relations with Somalia.

• It carries strategic implications for Red Sea–Gulf of Aden
maritime security and wider great power competition.

Somaliland’s Recognition

Somaliland –

• Somaliland is a self-declared sovereign state in the Horn of
Africa, internationally treated as an autonomous region of
Somalia, but functioning as a de facto independent entity since
1991.

• Geographically, it lies on the southern coast of the Gulf of
Aden, bordering Djibouti to the northwest, Ethiopia to the
south and west, and eastern Somalia.

• The capital is Hargeisa, and the population is approximately
6.2 million (as of 2026).

Somaliland’s Recognition


• The region has a 460-mile coastline along the Gulf of Aden
and is close to the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a key global
maritime chokepoint.

• The Port of Berbera is a major strategic asset and has seen
significant investment from the UAE.

• Somaliland is currently led by President Abdirahman
Mohamed Abdullahi, who won the 2024 presidential election.

Somaliland’s Recognition



• It is often described as an “oasis of stability” in the Horn of
Africa, compared to prolonged instability in southern Somalia.

• The currency of Somaliland is the Somaliland shilling (Sl.Sh.
or SLSH). However, due to its lack of international recognition
and the currency's low value, the United States dollar is widely
accepted and often preferred for larger transactions.

Somaliland’s Recognition

History of Somaliland –

• Isaaq Sultanate was established in the mid-18th century
and ruled much of present-day Somaliland until European
intervention.

• Between 1821–1884, Muhammad Ali Pasha of Egypt
established a brief Egyptian presence in coastal towns such as
Berbera.

• The United Kingdom created the British Somaliland
Protectorate after signing treaties with local clans between
1884–1886, mainly to secure meat supplies for Aden.

Somaliland’s Recognition

• From 1900–1920, the Dervish movement led by
Mohammed Abdullah Hassan fought British rule; it ended
after the Royal Air Force bombed the Dervish capital Taleh.

• During World War II, Italy occupied British Somaliland
in August 1940, but British forces retook it in 1941.

• On June 26, 1960, British Somaliland became
independent as the State of Somaliland, gaining recognition
from 35 countries.

Somaliland’s Recognition

• On July 1, 1960, it merged with Italian Somaliland to form the
Somali Republic, but northern regions soon felt politically
marginalised by Mogadishu.

• After Siad Barre seized power in 1969, repression intensified; the
Somali National Movement (SNM) was formed in 1981, followed
by mass violence including the 1988 carpet bombing of Hargeisa.

• On May 18, 1991, after the collapse of the Barre regime, leaders
met in Burao and re-declared independence, restoring the borders of
British Somaliland. Since 1991, Somaliland has built stable
institutions.

Somaliland’s Recognition

What brings this in news?

• On December 26, 2025, Israel became the first UN
member state to formally recognise Somaliland as an
independent and sovereign nation, establishing full diplomatic
ties and reshaping Horn of Africa geopolitics.

• The recognition was sealed through a joint declaration
signed by Benjamin Netanyahu, Gideon Sa’ar, and
President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, framed in the
spirit of the Abraham Accords, with Somaliland expressing
readiness to join and a formal signing expected in early 2026.

Somaliland’s Recognition

• Both sides agreed to exchange ambassadors and open
embassies in Hargeisa and Jerusalem, alongside immediate
cooperation in agriculture, healthcare, technology, and
economic development.

• Strategically, the move gives Israel a foothold near the Bab
al-Mandeb Strait, strengthening maritime security and
potentially enabling intelligence or military coordination against
Iran-backed Houthi threats from Yemen.

• The recognition is also viewed as a counter to regional rivals
such as Turkey, which maintains strong military and commercial
influence in Somalia.

Somaliland’s Recognition

• Major controversy surrounds allegations of a deal involving
Palestinian resettlement from Gaza to Somaliland; while
initially denied, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud
later claimed it was a secret condition.

• The decision has been rejected by the African Union, Arab
League, EU, Turkey, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia, all reaffirming
Somalia’s territorial integrity.

• At an emergency UN Security Council meeting, the United
States defended Israel’s right to the move but reiterated that its
own policy continues to recognise Somalia’s sovereignty and
borders.
